stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many planners assume that converting curbside parking into protected bike lanes reduces driving across an entire district. A study of the Eastgate district of Halvorsen complicates that view. After a lane opened, residents living within 500 meters of it made fewer car trips shorter than 3 kilometers, while their car trips longer than 3 kilometers held steady. Residents living farther away showed no change in either kind of trip. These results suggest that if the city extended the lane so that a neighborhood now 2 kilometers away fell within 500 meters of it, that neighborhood's residents would likely ______
choices: make fewer car trips both shorter and longer than 3 kilometers than they did before the extension.
make about as many car trips of every length as before, as the study's more distant residents did.
make fewer car trips shorter than 3 kilometers while making about as many longer car trips as before.
make about as many car trips shorter than 3 kilometers while making fewer longer car trips than before.
explanation: Write the finding as an arrow: living within 500 meters of the lane leads to fewer short car trips (under 3 kilometers) and no change in long ones. Living farther away leads to no change at all. The extension moves the neighborhood from the far group into the near group, so its residents should now follow the near-group pattern. That means fewer short trips and steady long trips. You have to carry both halves of the near-group result forward, not just the fact that the neighborhood is now close.

A.why: You saw the key point, that the neighborhood joins the near group, and then finished it the obvious way: near the lane means less driving. But even near residents kept making long trips at the same rate. This choice brings back the popular view that the passage sets out to correct.

B.why: You applied the result for the wrong group. 'No change' describes residents who live far from the lane. After the extension, this neighborhood lives near it, so the far-group result no longer applies.

D.why: You got the group right but swapped the trip lengths. In the study, short car trips fell and long ones held steady. This choice reverses that, which is the mirror-image trap this question type is built around.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Mycorrhizal fungi colonize crop roots and extend them into the surrounding soil, and some seed suppliers market fungal inoculants as a general boost to yield. Field trials by agronomist Inés Valdecasas suggest the benefit is narrower. In plots low in soil phosphorus, inoculated sorghum outyielded uninoculated sorghum in drought years but not in years of normal rainfall. In phosphorus-rich plots, inoculation made no difference in either kind of year. The trials imply that if a grower with phosphorus-rich soil stopped fertilizing until soil phosphorus became low, the grower's inoculated sorghum would likely ______
choices: outyield uninoculated sorghum in both drought years and years of normal rainfall.
outyield uninoculated sorghum in drought years but not in years of normal rainfall.
outyield uninoculated sorghum in years of normal rainfall but not in drought years.
yield about the same as uninoculated sorghum in drought years and normal years alike.
explanation: Write the finding as an arrow: low soil phosphorus plus drought leads to higher yields from inoculated sorghum. Low phosphorus plus normal rain leads to no gain. High phosphorus leads to no gain in any year. Once the grower stops fertilizing, the soil moves from the phosphorus-rich group to the low-phosphorus group. The low-phosphorus pattern then applies: inoculation helps in drought years and makes no difference in normal years.

A.why: You correctly moved the grower into the low-phosphorus group but forgot the second condition. Even in low-phosphorus plots, inoculation helped only during drought. Claiming a gain in every year repeats the marketing claim that the passage calls too broad.

C.why: You got the group right but reversed the condition. In low-phosphorus plots, the gain came in drought years, not in years of normal rainfall. This choice is the mirror image of the correct answer.

D.why: You applied the result for the grower's old soil. 'No difference' describes phosphorus-rich plots, but once the grower stops fertilizing, the soil becomes low in phosphorus, and a different result applies.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Cartographers have long assumed that printing more contour lines makes a topographic map easier to read. Psychologist Lena Okafor's work complicates that assumption. In her study, hikers judged the steepness of slopes shown on maps. Experienced hikers' estimates tracked the contour interval printed in each map's legend, but novices' estimates tracked only how tightly the lines were packed, whatever the interval. Okafor's findings therefore suggest that if a park reissued its trail maps with the contour interval reduced from 20 meters to 10 meters, ______
choices: novice hikers would likely judge the park's slopes to be steeper than before, while experienced hikers' judgments would change little.
experienced hikers would likely judge the park's slopes to be steeper than before, while novice hikers' judgments would change little.
novice hikers would likely judge the park's slopes to be less steep than before, while experienced hikers' judgments would change little.
novice and experienced hikers alike would likely judge the park's slopes to be steeper than before, since both would see more lines.
explanation: Write the finding as an arrow: tighter line packing → judged steeper → novices only. Halving the interval puts twice as many lines on the same terrain, so the lines sit closer together. Novices read that packing as steepness, so they judge the slopes steeper. Experienced hikers read the legend, notice the new interval and correct for it, so their judgments barely move.

B.why: You got the direction right but gave the effect to the wrong group. Experienced hikers used the printed interval, so the denser lines wouldn't fool them. Only the novices go by packing.

C.why: You picked the right group but reversed the direction, probably because a smaller interval sounds like a more precise map. More precision doesn't help the novices, who ignore the interval. They only see lines packed closer, and that reads as steeper.

D.why: You applied the change to everyone. The passage says experienced hikers' estimates followed the legend, so they would adjust for the new interval rather than be misled by the extra lines.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: It is often argued that workers in low-income neighborhoods look for jobs close to home because they prefer short commutes. A study by economist Tomás Herrera points elsewhere. When a city began handing out free transit passes, workers without cars widened the area in which they applied for jobs by nearly 40 percent, whereas the search areas of workers who owned cars were essentially unchanged. If the same passes were handed out in two neighborhoods, Eastvale, where most households own a car, and Millbrook, where few do, Herrera's findings suggest that ______
choices: job searches would likely widen more in Eastvale than in Millbrook.
job searches would likely widen more in Millbrook than in Eastvale.
job searches would likely narrow more in Millbrook than in Eastvale.
job searches would likely widen by similar amounts in both places.
explanation: The arrow is: free pass → wider job search → workers without cars only. Millbrook is the neighborhood where most households have no car, so most of its workers are in the group the pass affects. Eastvale is mostly car owners, whose search areas didn't change. So searches would widen more in Millbrook.

A.why: You got the direction right but matched the effect to the wrong neighborhood. Eastvale is mostly car owners, and car owners' search areas didn't change.

C.why: You chose the right neighborhood but reversed the effect. The pass made travel cheaper, and carless workers responded by searching more widely, not less.

D.why: You ignored the split the passage sets up. The pass had a large effect on one group and almost none on the other, so neighborhoods with very different car ownership shouldn't respond the same way.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Because the skin produces vitamin D when exposed to sunlight, people's vitamin D levels tend to fall during months with little sun. Nutrition scientist Priya Raman gave vitamin D supplements to adults and measured how much dietary calcium they absorbed. Among participants who began with low vitamin D levels, calcium absorption rose substantially; among those who began with adequate levels, it barely changed. Raman's results suggest that if the same supplement trial were run twice at a northern site, once in midwinter and once in midsummer, ______
choices: the average gain in calcium absorption would likely be larger in the midsummer trial.
the average loss in calcium absorption would likely be larger in the midwinter trial.
the average gain in calcium absorption would likely be similar in the two trials.
the average gain in calcium absorption would likely be larger in the midwinter trial.
explanation: This takes two steps. First, from the opening sentence: little sun in midwinter → more people start the trial with low vitamin D. Second, from the finding: supplement → higher calcium absorption → only in people who start low. A midwinter trial has more participants in the group that responds, so its average gain should be larger.

A.why: You linked sunshine to benefit when the link runs the other way. Summer sun keeps vitamin D levels adequate, and people with adequate levels gained almost nothing from the supplement.

B.why: You picked the right season but reversed the direction. The supplement raised absorption in people who started low. Nothing in the passage says it lowered absorption for anyone.

C.why: You used the finding but skipped the first sentence, which says vitamin D levels change with the seasons. Because of that, the two trials would start with different mixes of low and adequate participants.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Surface surveys let archaeologists estimate a buried settlement's extent from the scatter of artifacts on a field. In experiments on ploughed land, however, Ingrid Solberg found that each season's ploughing carried small objects, such as beads and stone flakes, several meters from where they lay, whereas large objects, such as grinding stones, hardly moved at all. Solberg's findings imply that if archaeologists surveyed a site that had been ploughed for decades, ______
choices: boundaries drawn from large objects would likely enclose a larger area than the settlement actually covered.
boundaries drawn from small objects would likely enclose a smaller area than the settlement actually covered.
boundaries drawn from small objects would likely enclose a larger area than the settlement actually covered.
boundaries drawn from either kind of object would likely enclose a larger area than the settlement actually covered.
explanation: The arrow is: ploughing → objects shifted several meters each season → small objects only. Over decades those shifts add up, and small objects spread out past the edge of the settlement. A boundary drawn around the small-object scatter would therefore cover too much ground. The large objects stay put, so they still mark the true edge.

A.why: You got the direction right but gave it to the wrong objects. The passage says large objects hardly moved, so they still mark the settlement's real extent.

B.why: You picked the right objects but reversed the direction. Being carried several meters season after season spreads the small objects outward, so their scatter grows.

D.why: You extended the effect to every object. The passage contrasts the two sizes on purpose: only the small ones were displaced.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Caffeine is widely assumed to give every endurance athlete a boost. Exercise physiologist Daniel Achterberg found otherwise: a pre-race dose improved cyclists' time-trial performance among those who rarely consumed caffeine but not among those who drank coffee daily, apparently because daily use builds a tolerance that fades after several weeks without caffeine. Achterberg's findings suggest that if daily coffee drinkers gave up caffeine for two months before a race and then took a pre-race dose, ______
choices: the dose would likely do more for their performance than it would have done without the break.
the dose would likely do less for their performance than it would have done without the break.
the dose would likely do no more for their performance than it would have done without the break.
the dose would likely do more for their performance than it does for cyclists who rarely use caffeine.
explanation: The finding gives you two arrows. First: daily use → tolerance → no benefit. Second: several weeks without caffeine → tolerance fades. Two months is more than several weeks, so these cyclists effectively move into the group the dose helps. The dose should do more for them than it would have without the break.

B.why: You reversed the direction, perhaps by treating the break as a loss of conditioning. The break removes the tolerance that was blocking the benefit, so the dose should help more, not less.

C.why: You noticed that daily drinkers got no benefit and stopped there. The question changes their condition, and the passage says tolerance fades after several weeks, so they no longer belong in the group the dose doesn't help.

D.why: The passage supports these cyclists recovering the benefit, not getting more of it than cyclists who never built a tolerance. That comparison needs evidence the passage doesn't give.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Astronomers often describe light pollution as a threat to all ground-based observing. Analyzing ten years of records from a hilltop telescope, Mei Tanaka found a narrower effect: on nights when the glow from a nearby town brightened the sky, the telescope recorded markedly fewer faint galaxies than usual, whereas its counts of bright galaxies did not change. Tanaka's analysis suggests that if the town replaced its streetlights with fixtures that send less light skyward, ______
choices: the telescope's counts of bright galaxies would likely rise, while its counts of faint galaxies would hold steady.
the telescope's counts of faint galaxies would likely fall, while its counts of bright galaxies would hold steady.
the telescope's counts of faint and bright galaxies would both likely rise, since the sky would be darker overall.
the telescope's counts of faint galaxies would likely rise, while its counts of bright galaxies would hold steady.
explanation: The arrow is: brighter sky → fewer galaxies recorded → faint galaxies only. The new streetlights make the sky darker, which reverses the condition, so the effect reverses too: faint-galaxy counts should rise. Bright-galaxy counts weren't affected by sky glow in the first place, so they should stay the same.

A.why: You got the direction right but swapped the groups. Bright-galaxy counts stayed the same even on bright nights, so a darker sky has nothing to restore for them.

B.why: You picked the right group but kept the original direction. Fewer counts went with a brighter sky. This change makes the sky darker, so faint-galaxy counts should go up.

C.why: You went back to the popular view that the passage opens with and then corrects. Tanaka found that sky glow affected only faint galaxies, so darkening the sky shouldn't change the bright counts.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Paving over land is usually blamed for worsening every flood downstream. Hydrologist Ruth Abernathy's records from a suburban river complicate that view. After its watershed was largely paved, peak flows from modest storms nearly doubled, but peak flows from the largest storms barely changed, because in those storms even unpaved soil quickly became saturated and shed water as fast as pavement did. Abernathy's data suggest that if the watershed's parking lots were rebuilt with porous paving that lets rain soak into the ground, ______
choices: peak flows from the largest storms would likely fall, while those from modest storms would change little.
peak flows from modest storms would likely fall, while those from the largest storms would change little.
peak flows from modest storms would likely rise, while those from the largest storms would change little.
peak flows from storms of every size would likely fall, by roughly the same proportion in each case.
explanation: The arrow is: paving → higher peak flows → modest storms only, because in the largest storms soaked soil sheds water as fast as pavement does. Porous paving lets rain soak in, which partly undoes the paving, so modest-storm peaks should come down. In the largest storms the ground under porous paving also fills up quickly, so those peaks should change little.

A.why: You got the direction right but gave it to the wrong storms, probably because the largest floods seem to matter most. The passage says paving barely affected the largest storms, so undoing it won't change them much either.

C.why: You picked the right storms but reversed the direction. Porous paving lets water soak in, which works against the paving effect. It lowers peak flows.

D.why: You went back to the 'every flood' view that the passage corrects. Abernathy's records show the largest storms responding differently, and the passage explains why.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many clinics schedule vaccinations whenever it is convenient, on the assumption that timing is irrelevant. Immunologist Kwame Asante's trial suggests otherwise for some patients: adults over 65 who received an influenza vaccine in the morning developed substantially higher antibody levels than those vaccinated in the afternoon, whereas among adults under 40, timing made no measurable difference. If a clinic serving a retirement community and a clinic serving university students both moved their vaccinations from mornings to afternoons, Asante's findings suggest that ______
choices: antibody levels would likely fall more among the students than among the retirement community's residents.
antibody levels would likely rise more among the retirement community's residents than among the students.
antibody levels would likely fall more among the retirement community's residents than among the students.
antibody levels would likely fall by about the same amount among both the residents and the students.
explanation: The arrow is: morning vaccination → higher antibodies → only adults over 65. Here the clinics move from morning to afternoon, the less favorable time, so the effect runs downward. The retirement community's residents are the older group, so their antibody levels would drop. The students are under 40, so timing doesn't affect them and their levels hold.

A.why: You got the direction right but gave it to the wrong group. Timing made no measurable difference for adults under 40, which is the students' group.

B.why: You picked the right group but took the direction from the finding rather than from the change. The finding favors mornings, and these clinics are giving up mornings, so older patients' antibody levels go down.

D.why: You applied the effect to everyone. The passage gives the timing effect only to older adults and specifically rules it out for younger ones.
